blocks.text: Necrotrap is an internet-based music genre and aggressive derivative of Trap Metal that originated from the SoundCloud rap underground in the early 2020s. The genre is built around heavily distorted 808 basslines with aggressive vocal delivery influenced by metal, incorporating Drum and Bass and Dubstep elements primarily in kick patterns and mixing approach.

The genre's production centers on 808 basslines pushed through heavy saturation and distortion to achieve maximum loudness while maintaining controlled mixing standards. Visually, the movement pairs degraded low-fidelity imagery with cyberwarfare motifs to build a combat-focused visual world. Even though Necrotrap was initially a brand for the collective NECROSOCIETY, the genre has since evolved into a decentralized online music movement centered on themes of modern warfare, horror/gore, and hacker culture. Unlike broader Trap Metal, where artists frequently use their music as an outlet for emotional volatility, Necrotrap's aggression is oriented toward shock value and world-building roleplay rather than emotional catharsis.

Necrotrap originated in the early 2020s as a direct reaction to the commercialization and perceived stagnation of the mainstream Trap Metal scene. Artists like Scarlxrd and collectives such as Spider Gang had popularized the fusion of heavy metal and rap, but early proponents of Necrotrap felt the sound had become formulaic and repetitive.

Contrary to early misconceptions attributing the term solely to Gorejit, the Necrotrap sound solidified in 2021 through the formation of the NECROSOCIETY collective. HXLX and Gorejit conceived the collective during a phone call, with Tsaruicide joining as part of that same founding conversation. The group did not initially set out to "invent" a named genre; rather, the style emerged as the three co-founders experimented with fusing the aggression of metal, heavy trap basslines, and electronic production techniques that deviated from the standard Trap Metal formula of the time.

The three co-founders—HXLX, Gorejit, and Tsaruicide—each contributed to shaping the genre's early sound and direction, with HXLX and Tsaruicide continuing to manage the collective to this day. As the roster grew to include new members, the "Necrotrap" descriptor was adopted to categorize their output, a sound born from collaborative experimentation rather than a singular coinage event.

As the Necrotrap sound spread beyond NECROSOCIETY's inner circle, unaffiliated artists on SoundCloud began adopting the label and aesthetic. Various underground producers like Dollscar, Torturechainn, M44A1, and HYPNXSIS produced music under the Necrotrap banner without direct collective involvement. IRAQ-A-HOLICS itself originated as a tag coined by NECROSOCIETY member FROSTTT before being formalized by HXLX into a standalone sister collective in 2023, further expanding the pool of artists working under the "necrotrap" label. Fanmade Necrotrap production tutorials and "type beats" have also proliferated on YouTube, further removed from the genre's collective-specific origin. While the groups NECROSOCIETY, IRAQ-A-HOLICS, and NECROWRLDWIDE remain the authoritative source of the genre, Necrotrap had become a decentralized online music movement defined as much by peripheral artists as by its founders.

The Necrotrap aesthetic is built around deliberately degraded image processing. Unlike the high-contrast or anime-inspired visuals common in mainstream Trap Metal, the genre uses grain, noise, sharpening, and stretching to create an intentionally low quality look. The style draws from three main visual territories: military and tactical imagery, including guns, vests, and combat settings; horror and slasher film elements including gore, body horror, and occult imagery; and hacking and cyberwarfare visuals. The overall look is meant to feel raw and aggressive, not clean or polished.

Necrotrap's reliance on tactical equipment, weapon schematics, and "Kill-Cam" visual effects is heavily influenced by first-person shooter (FPS) gaming culture and military simulation media. Many of the transgressive themes and titles are rooted in the 'edgy' humor and roleplay prevalent in 2010s-era gaming lobbies (such as Call of Duty or Counter-Strike), where militaristic jargon is recontextualized as a fictional persona rather than an actual political statement.

During the genre's early days (circa 2020-2022), the aesthetic also incorporated clay figures created by artist bezbique depicting mutilated or armed avatars. This remains a legacy motif, though the contemporary style has moved toward darker and more grounded imagery across all three visual themes.

Vocal delivery in Necrotrap is aggressive and raw, drawing its style primarily from metal influence. The core techniques include yelling, screaming, vocal frying, whispered delivery, and heavily distorted layering. Vocals are not clean or overproduced — the raw quality is intentional and central to the genre, alongside the 808s and percussion patterns.
Unlike traditional rap flows, vocals serve as a primary element of every track. While heavily processed and sometimes layered, they remain a central focus rather than background texture.

The genre's production is described as controlled distortion. Producers push 808 basslines to their limit using saturation plugins to achieve maximum loudness and texture without the unwanted artifacts of accidental clipping. Percussion patterns frequently deviate from standard trap arrangements, incorporating elements from Dubstep and Drum and Bass (DnB), specifically in kick patterns and mixing approach. Reese bass textures and industrial snares appear occasionally but are not a defining element of the sound.

Atmospheric elements contribute to the genre's "warfare" aesthetic. Tracks often feature samples from military shooters (e.g., Call of Duty), action films, and combat documentaries used as intros, outros, or ambient texture. Even though some producers utilize Memphis rap samples (a subgenre occasionally referred to as "Necrophonk"), the typical sound is meant to hit like a soundtrack from a slasher film or a violent video game.

Necrotrap is frequently conflated with the broader SoundCloud trap metal scene, and algorithmically generated genre-mapping tools such as Every Noise at Once (which directly informs Spotify's algorithm) have compounded this by grouping Necrotrap alongside artists with no direct connection to NECROSOCIETY or its associated sound. While fanbases for these scenes overlap and artists have crossed paths through collaborations and shared shows/platforms, Necrotrap was never intended to be a catch-all term for aggressive, horror-themed, or violent SoundCloud rap.

Artists associated with the collective GORE STREET, for instance, are commonly mislabeled as Necrotrap despite typically self-identifying under separate labels such as "Horrorcore." Likewise, artists working within general Trap Metal, such as Teenage Disaster or Afourteen, are sometimes grouped under the Necrotrap label despite bearing little resemblance to the genre's defining production and vocal techniques. Collectives such as Spider Gang, Hysteria, KARMAMØB, trtureprn, IDØL, АГОНИЯ, etc. have faced similar mislabeling, despite lyrical content, vocals, and production distinct from Necrotrap's. This largely stems from surface-level similarities: shared distorted production, overlapping listener bases, and a general aesthetic of aggression that algorithmic classifiers and casual listeners alike tend to flatten into a single category.

Part of the confusion also stems from Necrotrap's origin as a name specific to NECROSOCIETY's own output. HXLX has clarified that while the term originated as a label for the collective's work, it is not exclusively restricted to its members — other artists have adopted the label for Necrotrap-inspired music. This distinction between originators and the wider self-identifying scene has itself been a source of ambiguity in how the term gets applied.

The most common criticism Necrotrap faces revolves around its use of paramilitary imagery and violence associated with real-world conflicts, specifically those in the Middle East, which critics perceive as glorification of terrorism. Because the genre's themes are heavily built around shock value, critics argue this can trivialize geopolitical trauma by presenting it through an "edgy" or "video game" lens.

A common stereotype holds that the genre is a product of white suburban American teenagers. In practice, however, major collectives like NECROSOCIETY are made up predominantly of European adults. This has not alleviated concerns regarding cultural appropriation: some critics argue that the use of warzone footage and specific religious terminology by artists disconnected from those conflicts aestheticizes real-world suffering.

In response to allegations of trivializing violence, members of the NECROSOCIETY collective have described the aesthetic as a deliberate reflection of "generational desensitization" to digital warfare.

The collective frames the use of militaristic and combat imagery as an extension of the horror genre rather than a political statement. Just as audiences consume slasher films for the thrill of fictionalized death, they argue, Necrotrap listeners process the horror of modern warfare through a similar lens of detachment and adrenaline. The imagery is described by Tsaruicide as "animalistic and sketchy on purpose," meant to evoke a specific visceral reaction as an immersive world-building exercise, not as commentary on any geopolitical events.
